title: How the human body changed: apes to us

intro.focus: Showing interesting evolutionary CHANGE across the human line and its living relatives, not a proven chain of direct ancestors.
intro.honesty: Images are the best current reconstructions, not photographs of the past. Relationships are shown as supported, candidate, or context; living apes are cousins, not ancestors.

taxa.summary: A well-known early ape, before any living ape lineage had taken on its specialised body. This is roughly where the ape story starts.
taxa.physicalChange: A tailless ape that still moved as an above-branch quadruped — none of the suspensory, knuckle-walking or upright specialisations of living apes yet.
taxa.behavioralChange: Tooth-wear microwear shows a diet of soft, sugary fruit, not tough food — picked carefully while moving through the canopy on a flexible, bending lower back rather than swinging. Males had much larger, more projecting canines than females, pointing to male-male contests over access to mates, an ape-typical social pattern.

pressures.change: Loss of the tail and a more upright trunk
pressures.pressure: Cautious climbing and feeding in the canopy favoured balance over a tail.
Male-male competition for mating access, before any living ape lineage had specialised away from this generalised body.

taxa.certainty: Solid as an early ape; not a proven direct ancestor of living apes.

image.creator: Paleoart, Wikimedia Commons
image.caveat: A life restoration of a closely related early Miocene ape (Proconsul) — Ekembo was formerly placed in Proconsul. Representative, not exact.

fossilSites.note: Skulls, teeth and partial skeletons of an early ape.

taxa.commonName: a late Miocene African great ape
taxa.summary: A large African ape living close to the time the gorilla and human–chimp lines were separating. Known mainly from a jaw and teeth.
taxa.physicalChange: A big-bodied great ape with thick-enamelled teeth — evidence that African great apes were diversifying near the gorilla and chimp splits.
observedTraits: known from jaw and teeth only
taxa.behavioralChange: Lived in dry, tough-leaved woodland rather than lush forest. Low, rounded molar cusps suggest a flexible diet — soft fruit and leaves day-to-day, with teeth tough enough to fall back on harder nuts and seeds when food was scarce, an early version of the fallback-feeding strategy seen later in Paranthropus.

pressures.pressure: A more seasonal, less predictable woodland food supply than earlier forest apes had, rewarding resilience over specialisation.

taxa.certainty: Useful context near the African-ape splits; too incomplete to be a named ancestor.

image.creator: Paleoart, Wikimedia Commons
image.caveat: Nakalipithecus is known only from a jaw; a representative Miocene great-ape reconstruction is shown.

fossilSites.note: Partial mandible and teeth.

taxa.summary: Gorillas are not our ancestors — they are cousins. Their line branched off the shared African-ape stem around 9 million years ago.
taxa.physicalChange: The gorilla line went large and ground-dwelling: huge body, knuckle-walking arms, and a big chewing apparatus for leaves and stems.
observedTraits: large gut and jaws for leaves
taxa.behavioralChange: Lives in stable family groups of 6-30 led by one or two silverbacks (often father and sons), who decide when and where the group travels and feeds. Diet tracks local forest: eastern gorillas lean on bulky leaves and stems, western gorillas eat far more fruit — flexibility within a basically bulk-vegetation strategy.

pressures.change: Large body and big chewing/gut system
pressures.pressure: Split from the shared African-ape stem during a period of shrinking Miocene forest; less abundant fruit favoured a body that could subsist on abundant but low-energy leaves and stems instead of competing for shrinking fruit patches.
Moving a heavy body efficiently across the forest floor.

taxa.certainty: A living relative shown to make the branching real — not on the human line.

image.creator: Wikimedia Commons
image.caveat: A photograph of a living western gorilla.

taxa.summary: Our closest living relatives. Their line and ours split from a shared ancestor roughly 7 million years ago — neither is a 'primitive human'.
taxa.physicalChange: The chimp line kept a flexible climbing-and-knuckle-walking body and forest-fruit diet, while staying smaller-brained than later humans.
taxa.behavioralChange: Lives in fission-fusion communities: a large group that knows each other but splits into small, shifting foraging parties day to day. Males stay in their birth community and build alliances with relatives; tool-assisted hunting (mostly by females, only at a few sites like Fongoli) tracks seasonal food scarcity rather than being a constant habit.

pressures.pressure: Forest life that mixes fruit trees with travel across the ground.

pressures.change: Flexible fission-fusion social system retained, not replaced
pressures.pressure: Staying in forest/woodland with a fruit-centred diet kept the shared ancestor's social flexibility useful, while the human line's move to bipedalism and bigger cooperative groups built on top of that same root.

taxa.certainty: A living relative, not an ancestor; our best living comparison point.

image.creator: Giles Laurent
image.caveat: A photograph of a living chimpanzee.

taxa.summary: One of the oldest fossils proposed to be on the human side of the split, found far west of the usual East African sites.
taxa.physicalChange: Small ape-sized brain, but with reduced canines and a skull base hinting the head sat atop an upright spine — the first whispers of bipedality.
taxa.behavioralChange: Lived along an ancient Lake Chad shoreline in a mosaic of gallery forest, savanna and lakeshore. Whether it walked upright is a live, unresolved fight: the skull suggested it to its describers, but a 2023-2024 re-analysis of the arm bone argues it looked more like a knuckle-walker's — current bones can't settle it either way.

pressures.change: Head balanced over the spine (hint of upright walking)
pressures.pressure: If real, the same patchy lakeshore/woodland mosaic later seen in Ardipithecus and Orrorin: scattered food patches reward some ground travel even before full commitment to it.
Shifts in diet and in male-to-male social signalling.

taxa.certainty: Debated — possibly the earliest hominin, possibly an ape near the split.

image.creator: John Gurche / Smithsonian Human Origins
image.caveat: Artist’s facial reconstruction; the skull is distorted and soft tissue is interpretive.

fossilSites.note: Distorted but fairly complete cranium, plus a femur.

taxa.summary: A fragmentary late-Miocene form whose thigh bone is one of the earliest hints of upright walking.
taxa.physicalChange: A femur built for at least some upright, weight-bearing walking — yet the arms still say 'good climber'.
taxa.behavioralChange: Lived in dry evergreen forest, not open savanna — undercutting the old 'savanna pushed us upright' story. Curved finger bones and arm shape say it still climbed regularly to forage, while the femur carried real bipedal loading: walking and climbing coexisted rather than one replacing the other. Teeth point to a plant-heavy diet like a chimp or gorilla's.

pressures.change: Thigh bone adapted to upright loading
pressures.pressure: Efficient travel between scattered food patches inside a forest, not escape from one — among the earliest concrete bipedal signals (~6 Ma), arriving 'unfinished' and staying that way for millions of years.

taxa.certainty: Bipedal signal is real; whether it sits on the human line is uncertain.

image.creator: Smithsonian Human Origins
image.caveat: Orrorin is too fragmentary for a species-specific face; a representative early-hominin reconstruction is shown.

fossilSites.note: Partial thigh bone showing bipedal loading.

taxa.summary: Sparse teeth and bones near the human–chimp divergence, showing early dental changes.
taxa.physicalChange: Canines starting to lose their ape-like honing edge, with a toe bone read as compatible with upright walking.
taxa.behavioralChange: Lived in densely-wooded habitat close to permanent water, not open grassland. A toe-joint angle suggests real toe-off push during walking, not just upright posture. Big molars and fibrous-food wear point to a tougher plant diet than chimpanzees' fruit-heavy one.

pressures.pressure: Dietary and social shifts away from ape-style canine display, moving in parallel with the earliest bipedal push-off mechanics rather than as a separate cause.

taxa.certainty: Real but sparse; relationship to later Ardipithecus is plausible, not proven.

image.creator: Smithsonian Human Origins
image.caveat: A representative Ardipithecus reconstruction; A. kadabba is known from sparse material.

fossilSites.note: Teeth and a toe bone.

taxa.summary: A remarkably complete early hominin showing that walking upright arrived piecemeal — not as a finished package.
taxa.physicalChange: A pelvis that allowed upright walking, but kept a grasping, divergent big toe for climbing — a true mosaic, unlike any living ape.
taxa.behavioralChange: Lived in woodland (not open savanna) as a varied omnivore — isotopes show fruit, nuts and maybe small vertebrates rather than grassland grazing. Striking near-absence of male-female canine size difference points to lower male-male aggression than typical apes, hinting at more cooperative or pair-bonded group dynamics.

pressures.change: Upright walking added without losing climbing
pressures.pressure: Woodland life that rewarded both ground travel and tree feeding.
Less energy/risk spent on male-male canine threat-display may have freed capacity for the bipedal foraging strategies that followed.

taxa.certainty: Strong as a species; an early hominin, but not a proven direct ancestor.

image.creator: Cícero Moraes
image.caveat: A 3D full-body model of Ardipithecus ramidus (“Ardi”); posture is fossil-based, the surface is a plain render.

fossilSites.note: Partial skull, pelvis, hands and feet.

taxa.summary: The oldest widely accepted Australopithecus — the genus that walked the African woodlands for over a million years.
taxa.physicalChange: Leg bones show more committed upright walking, while the jaws and teeth stay large and primitive.
taxa.behavioralChange: Lived across a real habitat mosaic — riparian woodland and floodplain grassland along rivers feeding a lake, plus drier woodland and shrubland patches — likely moving between quite different micro-habitats rather than staying in one setting. Long forearms and wrist features say it still climbed regularly even with a more committed ground-walking gait than Ardipithecus.

pressures.pressure: A shift toward more open woodland/grassland than Ardipithecus's denser forest rewarded efficient ground travel between scattered resource patches across a more open mosaic.
Harder, grittier foods as habitats opened up.

taxa.certainty: Strong species; close to the ancestry of later australopiths. A 2019 skull (MRD) complicated the tidy hand-off story, though: it shows anamensis and afarensis actually coexisted for at least 100,000 years rather than one cleanly replacing the other, so 'anamensis became afarensis' is closer to a gradual, overlapping population split than a single line crossing a finish line.

image.creator: Paleoart, Wikimedia Commons
image.caveat: A representative australopith facial reconstruction; the near-complete MRD cranium informs the real species.

fossilSites.note: Nearly complete cranium.

taxa.summary: The famous 'Lucy' species — clearly bipedal on the ground, yet still built to climb, and still small-brained.
taxa.physicalChange: A fully bipedal pelvis, knee and heel-strike (and footprints to prove it), combined with long arms and curved fingers for climbing.
taxa.behavioralChange: Walked with a real but non-modern gait — more flexed limbs at footstrike than living humans, and ankle bones still closer to apes than us — while feeding flexibly: isotopes show individuals ranging from heavily forest-fed to heavily open-ground-fed within the same population. The 3.6-million-year-old Laetoli trail also shows two individuals walking side-by-side with synchronised steps, hinting at coordinated small-group movement.

pressures.change: Walking established before the brain grew
pressures.pressure: Efficient ground travel between scattered, variable food patches mattered earlier than big brains did.

pressures.change: Wide individual dietary flexibility retained in one population
pressures.pressure: That range (some more forest-fed, some more open-ground-fed) plausibly set up the next split: descendants could specialise in opposite directions — mechanical fallback-feeding (Paranthropus) vs. tool-assisted higher-quality foraging (Homo).

taxa.certainty: Very well sampled; close to the source of later lineages.

image.creator: California Academy of Sciences (model)
image.caveat: A fleshed museum model (the ‘Selam’ individual); body proportions are fossil-based, soft tissue interpretive.

fossilSites.note: ~40% of one skeleton.
Direct evidence of upright walking.

taxa.summary: A flat-faced, small-brained skull from the same Turkana basin, the same age as early Australopithecus afarensis — if it really is a separate species, hominin diversity existed already at Lucy's own moment, not just after her.
taxa.physicalChange: A notably flat lower face and smaller molars than afarensis, with less-projecting brow ridges — a different facial architecture from its far more famous contemporary, though the skull is crushed and distorted enough that this reading is contested.
taxa.behavioralChange: Known almost entirely from one damaged skull (KNM-WT 40000) and a few fragments, so there is essentially no direct evidence of movement or social life. Tooth enamel is more informative than the crushed skull, though: isotope measurements show a genuinely wide diet, from almost pure C3 (forest/fruit) to heavily C4 (grass/sedge) foods — real dietary evidence, even while the face shape itself stays contested (some read it as a different feeding strategy from afarensis, others as meaningless distortion).

pressures.change: A flatter face and smaller molars than the neighboring afarensis population
pressures.pressure: Unclear. It could reflect a genuinely different dietary or ecological niche occupied alongside afarensis in the same basin, or it could be ordinary variation within one species that a crushed skull makes look distinctive. The sample is too small and damaged to decide either way.

taxa.certainty: Highly disputed, not just under-studied. Some researchers treat platyops as a genuinely separate hominin sharing the landscape with afarensis; others argue the type skull is simply a distorted afarensis individual and doesn't justify a new genus. Kept here specifically to be honest that 'multiple lineages coexisted' is itself an uncertain claim at this particular branch point, not a settled fact like the later Homo split.

image.creator: Ing. Pavel Švejnar
image.caveat: A museum cast model of the KNM-WT 40000 skull (Anthropos Museum, Brno), not the original fossil; the original is heavily crushed and distorted, which is part of why the species' validity is disputed.

fossilSites.note: Distorted but relatively complete cranium.

taxa.summary: The first early human relative ever found in Africa (the 1924 Taung Child), showing the lineage had spread south.
taxa.physicalChange: A rounder skull and slightly larger brain than Lucy's species, with a less projecting face — but still an australopith body.
taxa.behavioralChange: Lived in South African cave country eating an almost entirely plant-based diet — a 2025 isotope study found animal protein made up under 10% of intake, leaning on gallery-forest resources rather than meat. More committed to ground-walking than the contemporaneous, more tree-climbing Paranthropus robustus nearby at Swartkrans, though it still used its arms for some climbing.

pressures.pressure: Solving food security through plant-dietary flexibility in gallery forest rather than through hunting or tool-assisted scavenging, unlike the path the Homo line later took.

taxa.certainty: Solid species; its exact place near the origin of Homo is debated.

image.creator: John Gurche / Smithsonian Human Origins
image.caveat: Artist’s facial reconstruction; soft tissue is interpretive.

fossilSites.note: Well-known adult cranium.
The 1924 discovery that started African palaeoanthropology.

taxa.role: Big-toothed sibling found with the oldest butchery evidence
taxa.summary: A short-lived side branch that combined a longer, more human-like stride with Paranthropus-sized teeth — and turned up in the same rock layer as the oldest confirmed evidence of stone-tool butchery.
taxa.physicalChange: Homo-like cranial proportions and a longer femur than Lucy's species (a longer stride), paired with a small, still-Australopithecus-sized brain and unexpectedly huge, thickly enamelled cheek teeth.
observedTraits: longer femur / longer stride than afarensis
taxa.behavioralChange: The same Bouri sediment layer that produced the garhi partial skeleton also produced antelope and horse bones with stone-tool cut marks and deliberately smashed-open marrow cavities — the oldest secure evidence anywhere of a hominin butchering large animals with tools, roughly 200,000 years before the earliest confirmed Homo fossil.

pressures.change: Large chewing teeth kept alongside the oldest known butchery evidence
pressures.pressure: Unlike its sibling Homo habilis, which shrank its teeth as tools took over food processing, garhi's teeth stayed big even as (if the same population made the tools) it started using stone flakes on carcasses — suggesting tool-assisted meat-eating and small-teeth-and-big-brain evolution did not have to arrive together, contrary to a tidy one-cause story.

taxa.certainty: The species itself is reasonably secure from the Bouri skull and skeleton. Whether garhi is the actual toolmaker is not: the cut-marked bones come from the same layer and time, not from garhi's own hand caught in the act, so several other contemporary hominins in the region can't be fully ruled out.

image.creator: Wikimedia Commons contributor 宜蘭第一公民
image.caveat: A photograph of the fossil collection at the National Museum of Ethiopia; not a life reconstruction — no vetted open-license life reconstruction of garhi's face exists yet.

fossilSites.note: Partial skull and associated partial skeleton, found with cut-marked animal bone.

taxa.summary: A spectacular side-branch that solved survival with giant teeth and chewing muscles, while early Homo nearby went a different way.
taxa.physicalChange: An extreme chewing machine: huge flat molars, thick enamel, flaring cheekbones and a bony crest on top of the skull for massive jaw muscles.
taxa.behavioralChange: Despite a skull built for hard-object feeding, dental microwear shows fine striations rather than the heavy pitting hard food leaves behind — boisei likely ate soft food most days, like a modern gorilla, and only fell back on tough, hard, low-quality food in lean seasons. Its anatomy reflects emergency survival capacity, not typical daily diet.

pressures.pressure: A bet on mechanical fallback capacity to survive lean seasons directly — the opposite strategy from sibling Homo habilis, which invested in tools to access higher-quality food instead. boisei's strategy worked for over a million years before ending without descendants.

taxa.certainty: A well-understood collateral branch — not a human ancestor.

image.creator: Smithsonian NMNH (photo: Ryan Schwark)
image.caveat: Chewing anatomy is fossil-based; hair, skin and eyes are interpretive.

fossilSites.note: Classic robust cranium.

taxa.summary: An early member of our own genus, with a bigger brain and smaller face than australopiths — but still a partly ape-like body.
taxa.physicalChange: Brain expanding (~510–700 cc) and face/teeth shrinking, even while arms and hands kept climbing-related features.
taxa.behavioralChange: Mostly scavenged rather than hunted: at many sites, stone-tool cut marks sit on top of carnivore tooth marks on the same bones, meaning predators reached carcasses first. Diet was a broad mix of fruit, leaves and scavenged meat/marrow, possibly organised around base camps with shared food processing.

pressures.pressure: Tools doing the work teeth used to: cutting and accessing higher-energy scavenged food — the opposite bet from sibling Paranthropus boisei's bigger-jaws fallback strategy, lower mechanical investment for higher cognitive/technological investment.

taxa.certainty: Real early Homo; its exact link to later Homo is debated.

image.creator: Cícero Moraes
image.caveat: A forensic reconstruction from incomplete fossils; soft tissue is interpretive.

fossilSites.note: Type specimen: jaw, teeth and hand bones.

taxa.role: Early Homo's other bet, alongside habilis
taxa.summary: A separate early-Homo population, living alongside Homo habilis in the same Turkana Basin, that grew a bigger brain without shrinking its teeth or picking up tools the way habilis did.
taxa.physicalChange: A notably larger braincase than habilis (about 775 cubic centimetres), a longer face, and larger molars and premolars than habilis — a bigger brain paired with a still-large chewing apparatus, rather than habilis's bigger-brain-smaller-teeth combination.
taxa.behavioralChange: Known mainly from one well-preserved skull (KNM-ER 1470) and a handful of other cranial fragments, so day-to-day behavior is poorly constrained. No stone tools have been found in the same layers as rudolfensis fossils, unlike the Oldowan association sometimes made with habilis nearby — though tools at shared sites can't be confidently assigned to either species.

pressures.change: A bigger brain kept alongside large, unshrunken molars
pressures.pressure: Unlike its contemporary Homo habilis, which shrank its teeth and leaned on stone tools to process food, rudolfensis grew brain size while keeping a robust chewing apparatus — a different early-Homo wager that didn't require giving up mechanical food processing to afford a bigger brain.

taxa.certainty: The KNM-ER 1470 skull and its distinctive proportions are secure. Whether 'Homo rudolfensis' is a fully separate species from Homo habilis, or represents extreme variation within one variable species, remains debated — the two are kept as contemporaries here because the anatomical contrast is real regardless of how the species boundary is ultimately drawn.

image.creator: Mauricio Antón
image.caveat: A life reconstruction of the head based on cranium KNM-ER 1470; soft tissue, hair and skin are interpretive.

fossilSites.note: Well-preserved cranium with an unusually large braincase for its age.

taxa.role: Southern robust cousin, africanus's own fallback specialist
taxa.summary: The southern-hemisphere echo of Paranthropus boisei: a separate robust lineage, likely descended from a population close to Australopithecus africanus, that bet on the same mechanical fallback-feeding strategy in a different country a continent's width away.
taxa.physicalChange: Very large, thickly enamelled cheek teeth, flared cheekbones and a sagittal crest anchoring powerful chewing muscles — despite a body that was actually smaller and lighter than its 'robust' name implies.
taxa.behavioralChange: Fine microwear striations rather than heavy pitting suggest robustus, like boisei, mostly ate soft food day-to-day and saved the big chewing apparatus for lean-season fallback. Worn, polished bone fragments at Swartkrans show it (or a hominin sharing its caves) used bone tools to break open termite mounds for insect protein — direct physical evidence of a foraging technique, not just a hypothesis from tooth shape.

pressures.change: A second, independent robust chewing apparatus, evolved separately from Paranthropus boisei
pressures.pressure: The same insurance-against-lean-seasons strategy that boisei bet on in East Africa reappears here in South Africa in a different population — suggesting the mechanical fallback-feeding solution was a repeatable answer to unpredictable Plio-Pleistocene food supply, not a one-off fluke of one lineage.

pressures.change: Bone-tool termite foraging alongside africanus's plant-heavy strategy at nearby sites
pressures.pressure: Unlike its likely South African ancestor Australopithecus africanus, which leaned on gallery-forest plant foods, robustus added a targeted insect-foraging technique on top of its chewing specialization — a second string to the same fallback-insurance bow.

taxa.certainty: The species and its chewing anatomy are very well documented from Kromdraai and Swartkrans. Its exact ancestor is not: africanus is the leading candidate, but no unbroken fossil sequence proves the link, and its relationship to the similarly robust East African boisei (shared robust ancestor vs. independent convergent evolution) remains actively debated.

image.creator: Nikhil Iyengar
image.caveat: An illustrated reconstruction of the DNH 7 female skull; soft tissue, hair and skin are interpretive.

fossilSites.note: Well-preserved cranium showing the chewing anatomy.

taxa.role: A second, independent attempt at the Homo transition
taxa.summary: A near-perfectly-dated South African population, probably descended from africanus, that mixed small teeth and Homo-like hands and pelvis with a small brain and long climbing arms — a second, independent candidate for 'transitional toward Homo', arising alongside (not necessarily ancestral to) Homo habilis.
taxa.physicalChange: Smaller premolars and molars and a more Homo-like face than africanus, functional pelvis changes linked to bipedalism, and a narrow upper chest / broad lower chest — all combined with a small brain and long, ape-like upper limbs.
taxa.behavioralChange: Walked upright regularly, but with an unusual gait — rolling each foot inward and landing on the outer edge, unlike the modern human pattern. Long arms and a small body suggest it still used trees regularly, even while its smaller, more Homo-like teeth hint at a dietary shift away from africanus's plant-heavy strategy.

pressures.change: Smaller, more Homo-like teeth than africanus, paired with a still-small brain
pressures.pressure: Instead of africanus's continued gallery-forest plant-foraging strategy or robustus's mechanical fallback-chewing bet, sediba's population shrank its teeth first and kept climbing — a third, distinct wager on how to leave the australopith body plan behind, running in parallel with (not necessarily descended from or ancestral to) Homo habilis's tool-first strategy further north.

taxa.certainty: The Malapa fossils (MH1, MH2) are exceptionally well preserved and precisely dated. Whether sediba is actually on the direct line to Homo, a dead-end cousin that merely resembles Homo by parallel evolution, or too late in time relative to habilis to be its ancestor is genuinely unresolved.

image.creator: Skull reconstruction by Kristian Carlson (courtesy Lee R. Berger / University of the Witwatersrand); photograph by Profberger
image.caveat: A reconstruction of the MH1 skull; soft tissue, hair and skin are not preserved and are not shown here.

fossilSites.note: A juvenile male (MH1) and adult female (MH2), unusually complete for this age.

taxa.role: Modern body, first to leave Africa
taxa.summary: The turning point: the first hominin with a tall, modern-looking body that ranged across continents.
taxa.physicalChange: Long legs, shorter arms, a narrow trunk and a bigger body and brain — built for long-distance walking and running on the ground.
taxa.behavioralChange: Walked huge daily ranges (the body plan fits endurance travel, though some pelvis fossils suggest power-running may fit just as well), made Acheulean handaxes for processing carcasses, tubers and nuts, and controlled fire by 1 million years ago (ash and burnt bone at Wonderwerk Cave). Spread out of Africa fast, reaching Europe and Southeast Asia within a few hundred thousand years.

pressures.pressure: Bigger foraging ranges and heat management in open country.
A richer, more reliable diet (meat plus tool-processed plant food) able to fuel the cost — locomotion and diet pressures reinforcing each other.

taxa.certainty: Strong as a broad grade; its many regional forms are debated.

image.creator: Public-domain illustration
image.caveat: A classic full-body illustration of Homo erectus; body is fossil-based, surface interpretive.

fossilSites.note: Near-complete juvenile skeleton.
Earliest secure humans outside Africa.

taxa.summary: A shock discovery: a small-brained human relative that survived surprisingly recently, found deep inside a cave system.
taxa.physicalChange: A mosaic body — human-like feet and legs for walking, but curved fingers, a primitive shoulder and a brain only a third of ours.
taxa.behavioralChange: Walked the ground and climbed; deep in the Rising Star cave, 2023 papers proposed deliberate burial pits and possible wall engravings, but a peer-reviewed rebuttal argues the evidence doesn't rule out natural causes (water transport, carnivore activity, a death trap) and that an easier historical cave route undercuts the 'carried bodies into danger' story. Whether the dead were treated with intention is a genuinely open question.

pressures.change: Small brain kept late in time
pressures.pressure: Surviving with a small brain this recently, alongside large-brained Homo, shows big brains were not the only viable strategy for this lineage's niche.

taxa.certainty: Securely a species; its origins and behaviour are actively debated.

image.creator: Cícero Moraes
image.caveat: A reconstruction from well-preserved skulls; soft tissue is interpretive.

fossilSites.note: Hundreds of bones deep inside the cave.

taxa.summary: A roughly one-metre-tall human relative that survived on an Indonesian island into surprisingly recent times.
taxa.physicalChange: Dramatically shrunk: barely a metre tall with a tiny grapefruit-sized brain, yet still walked upright and made tools.
taxa.behavioralChange: Cut marks on dwarf-Stegodon and giant-rat bones show organised carcass processing with an Oldowan-style toolkit, alongside tough, fibrous plant chewing — a mixed, demanding diet on a resource-limited island shared with other dwarfed and giant fauna.

pressures.pressure: Long isolation, limited food and few predators favoured smaller bodies (island dwarfism) — and the same pressure independently produced a second, unrelated dwarfing event in modern humans on Flores much later, showing the pressure itself does the work, not shared ancestry.

taxa.certainty: A real species; likely a dwarfed descendant of an earlier Homo such as erectus.

image.creator: Cícero Moraes
image.caveat: Forensic facial approximation of the ‘Hobbit’; soft tissue is interpretive.

fossilSites.note: Partial skeleton of a ~1 m adult.

taxa.summary: The broad, big-brained populations that gave rise to us, Neanderthals and Denisovans — the fork before the final three branches.
taxa.physicalChange: Brains as large as modern ones in a still-robust, heavy-browed skull and a powerful body.
taxa.behavioralChange: Capable of coordinated big-game hunting: the Schöningen site (Germany) preserves 9 engineered wooden spears used to kill dozens of horses at once, with fires built nearby apparently for cooking and group gathering afterward (though no hominin bones were found there, so the exact species is uncertain — it may be this grade or early Neanderthals). Built simple shelters rather than relying only on natural ones.

pressures.pressure: Planning-heavy hunting, fire use and social coordination across variable Ice-Age climates outpacing skeletal modernisation — the shared behavioral toolkit that sapiens, Neanderthals and Denisovans each later built on differently.

taxa.certainty: Useful population-grade; the single species label is disputed.

image.creator: Cícero Moraes
image.caveat: One face cannot represent all Middle Pleistocene Homo; soft tissue is interpretive.

fossilSites.note: Robust African cranium.

taxa.summary: Not primitive humans but a close sibling species — and many living people carry their DNA.
taxa.physicalChange: A stocky, powerful, cold-adapted body with a long low skull, big nose and a brain as large as ours.
taxa.behavioralChange: Isotopes show near-total carnivory, getting almost all protein from animal sources like a top predator — but dental calculus reveals real plant intake too, including cooked starches. The Shanidar 1 individual survived blindness and an amputated forearm into middle age, only possible with sustained group care (though the famous 'buried with flowers' story specifically has never been substantiated).

pressures.pressure: Surviving repeated Ice-Age cold in Europe and Asia, with biology (broad trunk, short limbs) layered under technological buffering (fire, hide-processing, likely clothing).

taxa.certainty: Very well known from fossils and genomes; interbred with Homo sapiens.

image.creator: Henryk Fudali (sculpture)
image.caveat: Body proportions are fossil-based; hair, skin and clothing are interpretive.

fossilSites.note: Adult who survived serious injuries.

taxa.summary: A whole human population first recognised from DNA, not bones — sister group to the Neanderthals.
taxa.physicalChange: Anatomy is still fragmentary (a finger bone, a jaw, some teeth), so much of their appearance is inferred from genes.
taxa.behavioralChange: Spread across an enormous range (Siberia to Taiwan, ~2,800 miles), adapting to wildly different environments. Butchered bones at Baishiya Cave (Tibetan Plateau, ~3,280m) show they hunted yak, snow leopard, wolf and pheasant — a high-altitude lifestyle reconstructed from faunal remains rather than their own skeleton. They also interbred not just with Neanderthals and modern humans but with a third 'superarchaic' ghost population ~700,000 years ago.

pressures.pressure: Living at low-oxygen Tibetan elevations — a rare case where we can directly observe the payoff: the EPAS1 gene variant still lets living Tibetans tolerate altitude today, passed forward through interbreeding after the species itself disappeared.

taxa.certainty: Genomically certain; many fossil attributions are tentative.

taxa.summary: Our own species — assembled in Africa from connected populations, then spread across the planet.
taxa.physicalChange: A high, rounded braincase, a flat face tucked under the brain, a chin, and a lightly built skeleton.
taxa.behavioralChange: Earliest fossils (Jebel Irhoud, ~315 ka) already had a modern face and teeth on a still-archaic braincase shape — anatomical modernity arrived in pieces. Notably, sites spanning ~150,000 years (Irhoud, Omo, Herto) show the same flaked-tool style despite modern faces: symbolic art and cumulative culture clearly lagged well behind anatomical modernity, not a single package.

pressures.pressure: Emerged from connected, dispersed African populations rather than one origin point; the long gap before symbolic culture appeared suggests the anatomical shift and the cultural shift were sequential, separate developments, not one cause.

taxa.certainty: Our species' reality is certain; no single fossil is 'the first human'.

divergences.label: The gorilla/chimp split
divergences.ancestorBaseline: Nakalipithecus was a generalist Miocene forest ape: a flexible diet of soft fruit day-to-day, with thick-enamelled teeth held in reserve for tougher food when fruit was scarce, living in dry, seasonal African woodland rather than lush rainforest.

siblingBullets.bullet: Gorillas abandoned the ancestor's fruit-first flexibility and committed to bulk: a huge body and gut built to subsist on abundant leaves and stems even when fruit ran out, trading food quality for a supply that's never scarce.

additionalContext.fact: The ~9 Ma split date shown on this timeline is a fossil-consistent estimate, not something genetics alone can pin down: genome-wide molecular-clock analysis finds mutation-rate variation wide enough that the gorilla split and the chimp/human split aren't cleanly resolved from DNA by themselves — the clean, separately-dated branches shown here lean on fossil calibration to do work the genomes alone can't.

siblingBullets.bullet: Chimpanzees instead kept the ancestor's flexible, fruit-centered foraging and built a social system around it — splitting into small, shifting parties to track patchy fruit trees, rather than gorillas' bet on always-available low-quality bulk food. Separately, they extended the ancestor's manual dexterity into real tool use — termite-fishing with stripped twigs, nut-cracking with stone hammers — something the bulk-feeding gorilla line never needed to develop.

additionalContext.fact: The single 'chimpanzee' branch shown here isn't the end of the story: chimps and bonobos themselves split from each other roughly 1-2 million years ago when the Congo River divided their range, and bonobos evolved a starkly different, far less aggressive, female-led social system on the south bank — genomic and behavioral evidence that even a lineage 'kept' unchanged at this branch point kept right on changing afterward.

divergences.confidenceNote: The anatomical split itself (gorilla bulk-feeding vs. chimp fruit-flexibility) is well documented. That a Nakalipithecus-like population is the actual shared ancestor is not — it's a plausible contemporary stand-in, not a demonstrated parent population.

divergences.label: Afarensis vs. the disputed platyops
divergences.ancestorBaseline: Anamensis was committed to ground walking (a bipedal shin bone) but kept a large, primitive jaw suited to tough woodland food, moving between gallery forest and floodplain grassland near water.

siblingBullets.bullet: Afarensis kept anamensis's bipedal commitment and its wide dietary flexibility (isotopes show individuals ranging from forest-fed to open-ground-fed within one population), and added synchronized group walking (the Laetoli trail) — betting on behavioral flexibility rather than anatomical specialization.

additionalContext.fact: A 2016 CT-scan study of Lucy's own skeleton found perimortem compression fractures — including a distinctive break pattern in her right humerus — consistent with a fatal fall from real height, most likely out of a tree. If correct, the individual held up as the icon of confident ground-walking still relied on trees enough to die falling from one (other researchers dispute whether the fractures happened before or after death).

siblingBullets.bullet: If platyops is a real separate lineage, it took the opposite path from afarensis in the same landscape: a flatter face and smaller molars point toward a narrower, more specialized feeding strategy instead of afarensis's broad flexibility — though the crushed skull makes this reading far shakier than afarensis's rich evidence.

additionalContext.fact: Despite the crushed skull, tooth enamel does carry real evidence: isotope measurements show platyops had a genuinely wide diet, from almost pure C3 (forest/fruit) to heavily C4 (grass/sedge) foods. A large co-existing primate in the same Turkana Basin landscape, Theropithecus brumpti, was already isotopically locked into the grassiest, most C4-heavy end of that same range — suggesting platyops's mixed diet may reflect ground already claimed by a bigger, grass-specialized rival.

divergences.confidenceNote: Afarensis's continuity from anamensis is well supported by shared anatomy and overlapping fossils. Platyops's place in this branch is speculative — it may not be a genuine separate branch at all, just a distorted afarensis skull.

divergences.label: Afarensis's five strategies
divergences.ancestorBaseline: Afarensis was a small-brained, confidently bipedal generalist that still climbed well and fed opportunistically across forest and open ground — no specialized teeth, no tools, no enlarged brain yet.

siblingBullets.bullet: Africanus stayed closest to afarensis's plant-based generalism, committing further to ground walking while leaning almost entirely on gallery-forest plant foods (under 10% animal protein by isotope evidence) — refining the ancestral diet rather than replacing it. Separately, it carried a slightly larger, more rounded braincase than afarensis — a modest step toward a bigger brain that arrived before any of afarensis's other descendants shrank their teeth or picked up tools.

additionalContext.fact: A 2015 study of the internal trabecular (spongy) bone in africanus's thumb and palm found a human-like loading pattern consistent with forceful, precision gripping — the kind associated with tool use — despite no confirmed stone-tool industry for this species. Internal bone structure responds to real mechanical loading during life, so this is physical evidence the hand may already have been doing tool-like work, with or without surviving tools to match it.

siblingBullets.bullet: Garhi kept afarensis-sized chewing teeth — even larger — but shows up in the same rock layer as the oldest confirmed stone-tool butchery, adding meat-processing technology on top of the ancestral plant-heavy dentition instead of shrinking its teeth first like habilis did.

additionalContext.fact: The 'oldest confirmed butchery' framing above is about cut marks specifically, not toolmaking overall: stone tools from Lomekwi, dated to 3.3 million years ago, predate garhi's own butchered-bone layer by roughly 750,000 years and predate the entire genus Homo — stone-tool manufacture was already an old technology, made by an unknown non-Homo hominin, by the time garhi's population (or whoever left the Bouri cut marks) used it on carcasses.

siblingBullets.bullet: Boisei went the opposite direction from garhi: it enlarged its jaw and chewing muscles into an extreme mechanical fallback system, betting that bigger teeth alone — not tools — would carry it through lean seasons.

additionalContext.fact: Carbon-isotope analysis of boisei's own tooth enamel complicates the microwear-based 'soft food most days' reading elsewhere in this dataset: it shows a diet of over 75% C4 grasses/sedges — more than any other hominin studied, and far more than its near-identical 'nutcracker' cousin Paranthropus robustus. Two evidence types point in different directions for the same skull design: short-term microwear says soft food at time of death, but the longer-term isotope signal says heavy grass/sedge reliance was routine, not just emergency fallback.

siblingBullets.bullet: Habilis bet against both africanus's plant-only path and boisei's bigger-jaws path: its teeth and face shrank while its brain grew, outsourcing food processing to stone tools instead of to anatomy.

additionalContext.fact: Whether habilis represents a new bet by our own genus at all is itself disputed: an influential 1999 reassessment argued habilis's body proportions below the neck — short legs, long arms, small stature — are so Australopithecus-like that the species arguably shouldn't be classified in Homo at all, proposing 'Australopithecus habilis' instead. On that reading, the brain-over-teeth strategy described here belongs to a bigger-brained australopith, not yet a member of our own genus.

siblingBullets.bullet: Rudolfensis, living alongside habilis in the very same Turkana Basin, made the opposite early-Homo bet: a bigger brain than habilis's, but molars kept large and no confirmed tools in its layers — growing brain size without habilis's tooth-shrinking, tool-assisted trade-off.

additionalContext.fact: A 2012 discovery strengthened rudolfensis's case as a genuinely separate species rather than just a large habilis individual: a juvenile partial face (KNM-ER 62000) shares rudolfensis's distinctive flat, broad features at a smaller, immature size — since juveniles shouldn't already show adult-scale sexual variation, a young rudolfensis-shaped individual is harder to explain away as ordinary variation within habilis.

divergences.confidenceNote: The anatomical divergence between these five is well documented and dramatic. Whether all five truly share afarensis as their single most recent common ancestor, rather than an earlier unsampled population, is not settled — treat afarensis here as the best-supported common reference point, not a proven parent. Habilis and rudolfensis are the exception with firmer footing: both are directly dated to the same Turkana Basin window (roughly 2.0–1.5 Ma), so their contrast is between true contemporaries, not just two branches of a shared deep ancestor.

divergences.label: South Africa's own split
divergences.ancestorBaseline: Africanus was a South African cave-country generalist, committed to ground walking, living almost entirely on plant foods with occasional climbing.

siblingBullets.bullet: Robustus doubled down on africanus's plant reliance by building a dedicated mechanical fallback system — huge chewing teeth for lean-season insurance — and layered a new foraging technique on top (bone-tool termite digging) rather than diversifying its diet.

additionalContext.fact: Isotope studies at Swartkrans show a co-existing giant baboon, Theropithecus oswaldi — much bigger than robustus — was already a committed grass-grazing specialist in the same landscape, while robustus's own isotope signal stayed mixed despite having comparable chewing hardware. One reading: the full-time grazing niche was already taken, leaving robustus's massive chewing gear as fallback insurance rather than a grazing strategy.

siblingBullets.bullet: Sediba instead shrank its teeth below africanus's and picked up a more Homo-like face and hands, wagering on a leaner, more processed diet and a body plan closer to the genus Homo, while still climbing regularly like its ancestor.

additionalContext.fact: A 2011 synchrotron scan of sediba's braincase found early signs of frontal-lobe reorganization toward a more human-like pattern — despite the brain itself staying small. That's a specific, complicating order of events: in this population, the internal wiring of the brain apparently began shifting toward the human pattern before the brain got any bigger, not as a result of it.

divergences.confidenceNote: Both descendants' distinct anatomy is well documented. That both specifically descend from africanus, rather than an earlier common South African population, is a reasonable but not fully proven inference — the fossil sequence has real gaps.

divergences.label: Shrinking vs. scaling up
divergences.ancestorBaseline: Erectus was a tall, long-legged, wide-ranging generalist — the first hominin body built for covering long distances on the ground across many different climates and continents.

siblingBullets.bullet: Isolated on Flores, floresiensis reversed erectus's size increase entirely, shrinking body and brain far below the ancestral range — trading erectus's long-range mobility for survival on a small island with limited food and few predators. Body size shrank, but toolmaking didn't: floresiensis kept knapping stone tools and butchering dwarf elephants, showing brain size and tool behavior didn't have to shrink together.

additionalContext.fact: A 2026 taphonomic study at Liang Bua found Komodo dragons — the island's only other large predator — consistently got first access to Stegodon carcasses, their tooth marks concentrated on the meatiest bones, while floresiensis's cut marks are confined to scraps (ribs, phalanges, skull fragments). The 'hobbits' most likely scavenged the dragons' leftovers rather than hunting or controlling carcasses themselves.

siblingBullets.bullet: Middle Pleistocene populations instead scaled erectus's body plan up further and grew the brain toward modern size, investing in bigger bodies and bigger brains rather than shrinking anything. That investment came with a separate behavioral shift: coordinated big-game hunting with engineered wooden spears and managed fire, plus simple built shelters — technology doing work anatomy alone couldn't.

additionalContext.fact: A saber-toothed cat, Homotherium latidens, directly competed with these hunters for the same prey at Schöningen — the pattern of bite marks shows hominins usually got carcasses first, not the cat, and researchers argue the engineered spears may have done double duty as a defensive weapon against this dangerous rival, not just a hunting tool. Hominins even reused one of the cat's own bones as a stone-tool-sharpening implement. Meat wasn't simply there for the taking; a real competitor had to be fought off to keep it.

divergences.confidenceNote: Floresiensis's dwarfing from an erectus-like ancestor is well supported by body proportions, though the exact ancestral population isn't pinned down. 'Middle Pleistocene Homo' is a deliberately broad grade label covering many regional populations, not a single lineage, so 'scaling up' summarizes several populations at once.

divergences.label: The last three-way split
divergences.ancestorBaseline: Middle Pleistocene Homo already had brains near modern size in a heavy-browed, robust skeleton, sharing a behavioral toolkit of coordinated big-game hunting, fire use and simple shelters across Africa, Europe and western Asia.

siblingBullets.bullet: In Africa, the population that became sapiens kept the ancestral brain size but lightened the skeleton and rounded the braincase, dispersing widely instead of specializing for one climate.

additionalContext.fact: Even 'anatomically modern' arrived in stages within our own species: a 2018 study of skull shape found sapiens crania only reached the fully rounded, globular braincase typical of living humans between about 100,000 and 35,000 years ago — meaning the brain's outward shape kept changing for over 200,000 years after the earliest Jebel Irhoud-era faces and brain sizes already looked modern.

siblingBullets.bullet: In Ice-Age Europe and western Asia, the same ancestral stock instead grew stockier and more heat-conserving, leaning on near-total carnivory to fuel a body built to withstand cold rather than to travel far.

additionalContext.fact: At Rio Secco and Fumane caves in the Italian Alps, cut marks on cave-bear and brown-bear bones (nearly 40% of one bone assemblage) show winter shelter itself, not just food, was a violently contested resource: Neanderthals fought and killed bears — including cubs and mothers — to take over the den. Surviving Ice-Age cold wasn't only a matter of a stockier body plus fire and hide-processing; getting the shelter to use those tools in required winning a fight with a large, dangerous rival first.

siblingBullets.bullet: Across Asia, from Siberia to the high Tibetan Plateau, a third population carried the ancestral toolkit into wildly different environments, including a documented genetic adaptation (the EPAS1 variant) for surviving low-oxygen altitude that neither Neanderthals nor early sapiens needed.

additionalContext.fact: The heaviest Denisovan genetic legacy today isn't near the Siberian or Tibetan fossil sites at all: modern Papuan and Melanesian populations carry the highest Denisovan ancestry of anyone alive (up to ~5% of their genome), from at least two deeply divergent Denisovan populations that had themselves been separated for 350,000+ years — implying an as-yet-unfound Denisovan population once lived somewhere in Southeast Asia/Wallacea, far from every known Denisovan fossil site.

divergences.confidenceNote: All three descendant lineages are extremely well supported by both fossils and genomes. 'Middle Pleistocene Homo' itself is a deliberately broad placeholder for structured, regionally varied populations, not one uniform ancestor — the single-species label is a convenience, not a settled taxonomic fact.

evolutionPoints.label: A generalist ape braces for leaner seasons
evolutionPoints.ancestorBaseline: Ekembo was a small, tailless canopy ape that picked soft, sugary fruit carefully while moving through the trees on a flexible lower back, with no specialised chewing or feeding equipment in reserve.
evolutionPoints.whatChangedBullet: Nakalipithecus kept Ekembo's arboreal, fruit-first habit as its day-to-day foraging style, but moved into a drier, tougher, more seasonal woodland than Ekembo's canopy and grew a much bigger body along with heavier, thick-enamelled molars as insurance for when fruit ran short — an early version of the fallback-feeding strategy later taken to an extreme by Paranthropus.
evolutionPoints.confidenceNote: Both taxa are securely dated fossils and the trait shift itself (bigger body, tougher teeth, drier habitat) is well documented. But roughly 10 million years and no continuous fossil sequence separate them — Nakalipithecus is best read as a plausible stand-in for what an Ekembo-like lineage became, not a confirmed direct descendant, so an unsampled branch hidden in that gap can't be ruled out. That gap probably isn't just an accident of where people have dug: a 2025 climate-modelling study ties this same window to East African Rift uplift and falling CO2 converting much regional forest to grassland, and apes living in the wooded pockets that remained fossilize poorly in acidic forest soil — the fossil silence may itself be a faint trace of the same habitat squeeze this entry's 'thicker teeth as insurance' story describes.

evolutionPoints.label: Tentative signals become a real mosaic body
evolutionPoints.ancestorBaseline: Kadabba is known only from sparse teeth and bones: canines just starting to lose their ape-like honing edge, and a single toe bone read as compatible with upright walking — suggestive, not conclusive.
evolutionPoints.whatChangedBullet: Ramidus turned kadabba's tentative signals into a genuine mosaic body — a pelvis that could really walk upright, while still keeping a grasping, divergent big toe for climbing that no living ape has. It also pushed kadabba's already-reduced canine dimorphism much further, nearly erasing the male-female size gap entirely, hinting that lower male-male aggression was already underway alongside the anatomical change.
evolutionPoints.confidenceNote: Ramidus itself is one of the best-documented early hominins. The direct line from kadabba is plausible — same genus, same region, sequential ages — but rests on very sparse kadabba material (teeth and one toe bone), so it's a reasonable inference from continuity rather than a proven parent-child fossil sequence.

evolutionPoints.label: The climbing trade-off gets abandoned
evolutionPoints.ancestorBaseline: Ramidus walked upright on the ground but hadn't given anything up for it: a mosaic body with a still-grasping, divergent big toe for climbing, living as a woodland omnivore.
evolutionPoints.whatChangedBullet: Anamensis gave up ramidus's climbing/walking compromise for full commitment: its leg bones show habitual upright walking without ramidus's climbing-optimised grasping toe. It also lived across a more open habitat mosaic — floodplain grassland and drier woodland alongside the river-forest ramidus preferred — while its jaws and teeth stayed just as large and primitive as ramidus's, showing the walking commitment arrived well before any dental change caught up.
evolutionPoints.confidenceNote: Anamensis's own anatomy (the bipedal shin bone, the primitive jaw) is very well documented, and it's widely treated as ramidus's likely successor given matching geography and unbroken sequential ages. Still, no single fossil trail physically connects the two — it's an inference from continuity and proximity, and a currently unknown side branch between them can't be excluded. Even ramidus's own starting point is less settled than it sounds above: the describing team read Aramis as closed woodland, but a separate isotope re-analysis of the same soils argues the carbon signature fits predominantly open wooded grassland instead — the same fossils and sediments, two specialist teams, two different readings of how open Ardi's world really was.

evolutionPoints.label: The last climbing anatomy is finally dropped
evolutionPoints.ancestorBaseline: Habilis had a bigger brain and smaller face than any australopith, but its arms and hands still kept climbing-related features like curved finger bones, and it mostly scavenged rather than hunted.
evolutionPoints.whatChangedBullet: Erectus dropped habilis's leftover climbing anatomy entirely — no more curved finger bones — finishing the shift to a fully ground-committed body: long legs, short arms, a narrow trunk built for covering serious daily distances. It also scaled habilis's brain-over-teeth bet much further, growing both a substantially bigger brain and a bigger body, and moved past habilis's scavenging pattern to controlled fire use and Acheulean handaxes built for processing carcasses.
evolutionPoints.confidenceNote: Erectus's own body plan is exceptionally well documented, and habilis is its most plausible immediate predecessor by anatomy and unbroken timing. But the transition spans well under a million years with sparse fossils in between, and 'Homo erectus' is itself a broad grade covering many regional populations — treat this as the best-supported reading of a real but incompletely sampled transition, not one single confirmed lineage. A 2013 skull from Dmanisi (Georgia) sharpens that caution further: at just 546 cc, its brain is barely bigger than habilis's, yet it was found alongside far larger-brained Dmanisi individuals as one population — leading its describers to argue habilis, rudolfensis and early erectus may be one variable, evolving lineage rather than three cleanly separate species, which would make 'habilis becomes erectus' less a single handoff than labels drawn across one continuously varying population.
